title: Vanity Fair
full_review:
Reese Witherspoon gives an assured performance as Becky Sharp among a stellar cast of top-flight English actors in Mira Nair's epic retelling of William Makepeace Thackeray's classic, "Vanity Fair" (Focus).

Dramatized many times on screen and television, this film is one of the most satisfying. The famous Miriam Hopkins version -- "Becky Sharp" from 1935 -- was notable for its pioneering use of the Technicolor process, and there was a notable "Masterpiece Theatre" telecast on PBS in 1972 with Susan Hampshire in the lead, among many other productions.

This production is beautiful to look at -- albeit the production design here is grittier than more genteel past productions. Director Mira Nair can be forgiven a somewhat revisionist slant as Becky is less the manipulative schemer as usually presented, but rather just a smart girl trying to survive in perilous times. Nair makes clear that Becky is operating in a world without a safety net. In that era, if you lost your money or position, it could be a very short fall to the gutter.

The story's a compelling one, which explains the piece's enduring popularity. Against a backdrop of the Napoleonic Wars, the young orphaned Becky (Witherspoon), daughter of a struggling artist, resolves to reinvent herself and make her way in the world. With confident serenity, she leaves the girl's boarding school where she's been treated like a slave, and goes to work for the upper-class but rustic Sir Pitt Crawley (Bob Hoskins), to whose household she brings clarity and order, thereby making herself indispensable. Before long, she ingratiates herself with the imperious Aunt Matilda (Eileen Atkins in a hilarious portrayal), and moves with the old woman to London.

Though Matilda loves imprudent romances in novels, she has a fit when Becky marries her nephew, Rawdon Crawley (James Purefoy), and disinherits him. (It is Atkins' indignant rising from her tub upon hearing the news that provides the film's only snippet of partial nudity.) Meanwhile, Becky's best friend, Amelia (Romola Garai), is enamored of the callous George Osborne (Jonathan Rhys-Meyers), whose imperfections Amelia refuses to see, marrying him in spite of paternal objections. She, in turn, is loved by the decent Dobbin (Rhys Ifans, superb in a completely different role than the recent "Danny Deckchair").

Eventually, Becky comes under the influence of the lecherous Marquess of Steyne (Gabriel Byrne), which threatens the impoverished but solid relationship with Crawley. Up to this point, Becky had thought she was adept at managing the false values of high society, but this time she's in over her head.
There's a whole gallery of fine performances by a stellar British cast, including Jim Broadbent as Osborne's unforgiving father, Geraldine McEwan as a busybody relation of the Crawleys determined to expose Becky as a sham, and others too numerous to mention.

But it's the captivating Witherspoon, seemingly on screen almost every minute, who rivets your attention. She has the uncanny ability to communicate what she's thinking at every turn, which makes her strategic rags to (not quite) riches story especially compelling. She also makes Becky's actions -- not always admirable -- plausible.

Nair gives the story the epic sweep it deserves, depicting a great canvas of balls, great crowd scenes with soldiers going off to war, a picturesque and grimy London, and other Regency period detail that encompassed the circus of life of that time. Some of the story is reminiscent of "Gone With the Wind," including one scene you'll recognize right away with its uncanny parallel to Margaret Mitchell's story.

Julian Fellowes, who won the Oscar for "Gosford Park," has written an intelligent screenplay in collaboration with Matthew Faulk and Mark Skeet, underscoring the theme: Who among us who achieves our desires is truly content?

If Nair pays homage to her own heritage by overemphasizing the Indian aspects of the story, there's no harm done to basic narrative. An Indian musical number -- straight out of Bollywood -- with Becky in the lead seems wildly out of place here, colorful and rather fun though it is. And the novel's ending is slightly changed, so that India figures more heavily in the plot's resolution.

Because of a slight flash of partial nudity, a little violence and some sensuality, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG--13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
